content: The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria, often referred to as The Global Fund, was established in January 2002 with the aim of significantly increasing global financial resources to combat these three major diseases. While malaria is technically endemic rather than pandemic, the fund addresses its widespread impact. It is the largest international financier of programs targeting malaria and tuberculosis, providing two-thirds of all global funding for these diseases. Additionally, it contributes 20% of all international funding for HIV/AIDS initiatives. Through its efforts in 136 countries, the Global Fund has been credited with saving 9 million lives. The origins of the Global Fund can be traced back to an article published in The Lancet in January 2001 by Harvard academics Amir Attaran and Jeffrey Sachs. They advocated for a substantial increase in foreign aid budgets for HIV/AIDS, compared to the levels documented in the 1990s. They proposed that funding should be directed toward projects designed and prioritized by the affected countries themselves, with these projects evaluated for their epidemiological merit by an independent panel of scientific experts. Attaran and Sachs also recommended that the funding mechanism provide grants, rather than loans, to the poorest countries, contrasting with the World Bank's approach, which was the largest multilateral HIV/AIDS funder at the time. The decision to create the Global Fund was made by world leaders during the 2001 G8 Summit in Genoa, Italy, following strong advocacy from United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan. The structure of the fund largely followed the recommendations of Attaran and Sachs. The first Secretariat of the Global Fund was established in January 2002, and Richard Feachem was appointed as its first Executive Director in July of that year. By December 2002, the fund had made its first disbursement to grantees. A significant milestone occurred in September 2005, when a conference in London mobilized €3 billion, representing just over half of the pledges made at the Gleneagles G8 Summit. The United States has contributed $700 million to the Global Fund but has diverted the majority of its AIDS funding to the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) to maintain closer control over fund allocation. The Bush administration faced criticism for prioritizing abstinence-only prevention programs, which lack evidence of effectively reducing infection rates, and for refusing to purchase cheaper generic drugs, which could have expanded treatment access compared to more expensive brand-name medications. The Global Fund is unique in its structure, being incorporated as a foundation under Swiss law. It operates as a public-private partnership but is often mistakenly associated with the United Nations due to its collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), which provides administrative support to the fund's Secretariat in Geneva, Switzerland. One of the fund's most praised attributes is its transparency, as it makes extensive information about its processes, including sensitive decision-making, publicly available on its website. Unlike implementing agencies, the Global Fund functions as a financing mechanism. It supports program monitoring through a Secretariat of approximately 250 staff members (as of 2006) based in Geneva. Program implementation is carried out by Country Coordinating Mechanisms, which are committees composed of local stakeholders, including government entities, NGOs, UN agencies, faith-based organizations, and private sector actors. Initial grant funding is awarded based solely on the technical quality of applications, as evaluated by the fund's independent Technical Review Panel. Continued funding is contingent on demonstrated performance, with grants initially signed for two years. Disbursements after the first six months are only made following proven results, and funding for subsequent years is approved after rigorous reviews of achieved outcomes. The Global Fund's performance-based funding model distinguishes it from other international agencies, such as the World Bank, WHO, UNAIDS, and bilateral donors, which typically oversee program implementation and focus on tracking expenditures rather than achieved targets. These organizations often extend programs indefinitely and employ large staff to assist with grant implementation. The Global Fund was established in response to the perceived lack of progress in addressing the three diseases under existing mechanisms. Since its inception, bilateral donors have pledged millions, and in some cases billions, of US dollars to support its programs. The fund's innovative financing principles are widely regarded as key to its success. By December 2006, the Global Fund had committed $7 billion to over 540 grants in 136 countries. In January 2006, Bono and Bobby Shriver launched the Product Red campaign, with proceeds directed to the Global Fund. In August 2006, the Gates Foundation contributed $500 million, describing the fund as one of the most important health initiatives in the world. In March 2006, Executive Director Richard Feachem announced his intention to step down, and in April 2007, Dr. Michel Kazatchkine was appointed as the new Executive Director. It is important to note that the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria is distinct from the Global Fund for Children, which supports grassroots organizations working with vulnerable children and youth worldwide.
